The cleanest division of labour on the board, because the lead is not a damage body at all and stops pretending to be: it stacks a permanent bonus die on both halves, keeps a revive and an outward heal, and holds Unarmoured Defence behind a shield. Aria is then the entire tempo half, and the bonus die lands where it matters most — on the Constitution saves that keep a persistent field standing for its full duration. The Bard also arrived in heavy armour, which is rare enough opposite a Monk to be worth saying.
Cloister.cost: Costs. Enemy action points come off more slowly here than anywhere else in the band. One body supports and the other deals two damage types, so the late-run resistance layers leave the pairing as a supporting Monk with nothing left to support. Both concentration slots are spoken for as well — the lead spends one of the pair's two to do any of what it does, and the blaster wants the other for its field.

vars.note: Swaps the storm for fire and a real skill floor, and the resistance problem moves rather than goes away.
A second Monk on the same clock, which raises the tempo and hands the pair no out-of-combat coverage at all.
Both halves then carry the same Monk subclass and the same Lore picks, so the second set of Expertise buys narrower ground than the first.

Moonward.verdict: Two independent sources of the same condition, and only one body converts it into damage. Full Moon is slot-free area Blind-and-Slow off the oath; Glaring Frost is a Constitution save inside a short-rest radiant burst that spares allies, spread three metres from every creature it catches at Ranger 15. Snow Blindness then charges radiant damage on every action a blinded enemy takes, which turns the Paladin's own free control into a damage engine it could never run itself. Underneath that sits prevention in two forms at once — Aura of Moonlight's flat minus-Charisma on every hit either body takes, and Divine Guardian halving all damage on the partner for ten turns off a short-rest charge — with Lunar Champion at 20 adding a Charisma-modifier bonus to every saving throw both bodies make, a third Reaction on top of Lone Wolf's second, and temporary Freedom of Movement.
Moonward.cost: The lead is prevention and never becomes a damage body, so the pair's entire attack routine is one sheet and enemy action points come off slowly — actions read 3 in every act. Skills are the holed axis: 3 in Act I and 2 across the back half, with no Expertise on either body and no third character to cover the traps and doors that arrive unannounced. Both halves also run their best work off short-rest charges — the burst, the blind and Divine Guardian all sit on the same clock — so anything that outlasts the charges finds the pairing running on plain weapon swings and an aura. Radiant sits on both sheets, and the type the punisher runs on is the type both bodies lose together.

vars.note: Buys the whole skill half — Guidance always prepared plus real Expertise — at the price of armour, on a body the aura has to chase.
Auras do not stack, so a second domain's outward temp-HP layer is worth more here than a second aura would be.
A free maximised area breath every round on a body that never spends a slot, in place of the punisher that feeds on the oath's own blind.

Anvilcant.name: Anvilcant & Psalter
Anvilcant.verdict: Reads as. The deepest out-of-combat coverage on the board and it is not close: the domain hands out the proficiency both mid-run gates are paid in, Guidance is already on the Cleric list, and two Lore packages stack Expertise and Jack of All Trades over the top, so every lock, check and ritual in the run has an owner. The aura then writes the paladin's Charisma onto every save the armoured Cleric rolls, which is the one stat a Wisdom body has no other route to, and the smites are the repeatable burst a support domain never had.
Anvilcant.cost: Costs. This is the slowest pairing here at removing enemy action points — a support domain beside a Bard that took its oath late, against a run that inflates the health of everything they are swinging at. Both halves also bought the same College, so the second set of picks buys ground the first already held, and the smite table refills only on the supply-priced rest. The aura body is the softer of the two and it is the one that walks forward, and the split casting stats mean no item lifts both DCs.

vars.note: Trades the second Lore package for prevention that never runs dry and hands the Cleric the whole utility budget alone — deeper defence, and the tempo problem untouched.
Bodies on the initiative order instead of an aura, which is the most direct answer this pairing has to its own slowness, and the face leaves with the Bard.

Fontspark.verdict: In a party of two, twinning a spell covers everybody, and the partner is the one body that most wants it: a half-caster whose engine only pays out at contact range, because Glaring Frost forces a Constitution save for Blind on every instance of Cold or Radiant damage and the Devotion block at characters 4–6 exists purely to make Divine Smite supply that radiant on demand. Twinned Greater Invisibility puts advantage on every one of those attacks and takes both bodies off the target list in the same cast, so the number of saves the room rolls goes up while the number of attacks coming back goes down. Twinned Death Ward from character 10 is prevention on both halves at once, Quickened Spell is the only reliable route to a third cast in a turn under Listo's bonus-action-spell rule, and Font of Magic converts short-rest pact slots into sorcery points and back to keep all of it fuelled.
Fontspark.cost: This is the softest reading in the band — resilience 0.55 in Act I, saves at 4 rather than 5, no aura writing a stat onto anything, light armour on one half and medium on the other, and no revive between them. The prevention is concentration-shaped and it all lives on one body, so the roll that breaks the Warlock's concentration strips both halves' invisibility at once. The Ranger is flagged on crowd fights, which means the pairing meets numbers a body down while its area reading is already a hole, and duration never leaves 2. Skills is the third hole: rung 3 in Act I, 2 for the rest of the run. Nothing before character 10 is the pairing it eventually becomes, and Act I tempo of 0.532 is what waiting costs.

vars.note: A melee half that never runs out and never asks for a slot, at the price of the Charisma the twinned buffs were sized around.
Two patrons, real burst and a genuine skill floor, and nobody at all standing in melee.
Expertise and always-prepared Guidance answer the skills hole, on a partner no better armoured than this one.

Bravura.name: Bravura & Fontspark
Bravura.verdict: Reads as. Two Charisma casters that never compete for a stat or an item slot, splitting the outward work cleanly: Combat Inspiration puts a die in the partner's hand that can be spent for armour class after the attack is seen, and Twinned Spell in a two-person party covers the whole party, so Death Ward lands on both bodies at once and Greater Invisibility makes both untargetable. Battle Magic adds a free weapon attack after every cast, so the Bard is a second attack routine rather than a caster standing behind one.
Bravura.cost: Costs. Durability is what paid for all of it — light armour and a draconic hit die on one side, medium armour and a shield on the other, no heavy armour and no aura anywhere because the oath levels land far too late for either. Nothing in the pairing answers a crowd at the rung the model wants, and the smite burst comes off the full-caster table, which refills only on the rest this run prices in supplies.

vars.note: A skirmisher carrying Guidance and Expertise, and the pair gives up the Twinned wards to get it.
A short-rest engine worth spending the die on, at the price of every skill on that side of the pairing.
A blessing and a revive in place of the wards, on a body that stands closer to the front.

Marginalia.name: Marginalia & Psalter
Marginalia.verdict: Reads as. Two Lore packages with an oath under one of them: between them the pair owns every check the run puts in front of it, and the aura writes the paladin's Charisma onto every save both bodies roll — which on a light-armoured ranged caster whose saves are its only real defence is worth more than any armour it could have worn. Both halves run the same stat to the cap, so one item lifts both DCs and the aura together, and the smites give the pairing the repeatable burst a Lore chassis never owns.
Marginalia.cost: Costs. Both halves bought the same College, so the second set of Expertise buys narrower ground than the first — depth where the pair was already deep and nothing at all where it was not. The aura is measured from where the paladin stands and the paladin is the mobile melee half, so the ranged body spends much of the fight outside the thing it is paying for. The smite table refills only on the supply-priced rest, only the pact slots come back sooner, and neither body wears heavy armour.

vars.note: Trades the aura and the duplicated Expertise for a short-rest burst engine, and leaves the Bard carrying the pair's entire out-of-combat budget alone.
The same pact and the same familiar twice over at range, with nothing standing where the paladin used to be.

Corsair.name: Corsair & Oathbound
Corsair.verdict: Reads as. The lead's damage floor is at-will and asks for neither advantage nor an adjacent ally, so it never competes for position with anyone — and this is the first partner it has stood beside that wears heavy armour, takes the hits and can raise it afterwards. The aura writes the paladin's Charisma onto every save both bodies roll, both halves run that stat to the cap, and the partner's smites come off pact slots that return on the short break rather than the supply-priced one.
Corsair.cost: Costs. Everything the aura gives is measured from where the paladin stands, and this lead's whole design is Cunning Action and stances that take it somewhere else — the pairing pays for a radius one half spends the fight leaving. Both bodies are single-target, so crowds are answered one creature at a time; the flourish resource is genuinely a long-rest one now that the critical range was sold; and the top of the partner's arcanum was the bill for the armour.

vars.note: A fire burst and a full skill package instead of the armour: it answers the crowds this pairing has no answer to, and gives up the front rank entirely.
A die handed over for armour class rather than a standing aura — reactive instead of always on, but it follows the skirmisher wherever it goes.

Portentblade.name: Portentblade & Lectern
Portentblade.verdict: Reads as. The other reading of this subclass went twenty levels of Eldritch Knight and never once touched the other character; three Wizard levels on the stat it already runs buy Portent, and Portent is the rarest thing in the model — a rescue that costs no action and no concentration, because it replaces a roll that has not happened yet. A partner's failed save simply does not occur. Lectern is the right side of that: a body whose own defence is a save-and-Guidance package rather than armour, so the dice land where they matter and Friar's always-prepared Guidance covers the checks a Fighter primary never learned.
Portentblade.cost: Costs. The fourth attack, and with it the top of the Fighter table — this body trades its damage ceiling for two dice a day and a slot refund. Portent is a long-rest resource on a chassis whose damage is at-will, so the halves run on different clocks and the good rounds are front-loaded into whichever fight you decide matters. Neither body wears heavy armour, and neither can heal.

vars.note: Trades Guidance and the Lore package for Peace's pair-wide save bond, which stacks with Portent rather than overlapping it.

vars.text: Against a save-DC boss: Portent is better spent forcing the enemy's failure than preventing your own, and the choice is made after seeing the roll.

Chorus.name: Chorus & Immolate
Chorus.verdict: Reads as. A patron built to be readable out of combat — Bard as the level-one class costs no second stat, and returns Dexterity and Charisma saves, Lore's picks, doubled Expertise and Jack of All Trades over everything else — sitting behind a heavy-armoured Cleric with an extra Action and a bonus-action strike. Bardic Inspiration also goes outward as spell damage under the modlist's own rule, so the support die is not wasted on a partner who would rather be hitting things.
Chorus.cost: Costs. Both bodies burst in fire, which is precisely the profile the endgame's layered resistances are built to punish, and the Cleric's maximised element is the same one the Warlock's expanded list is made of. Durability is the hole on the ranged half, which traded the domain's heavy armour for its skills, and those skills clear two acts and then read at nothing — so the coverage the whole dip was bought for expires before the run does.

vars.note: A short-rest burst engine that shares no damage type with the patron, and no armour on either side of the pairing.
An Intelligence caster with two slot tables, so the pair stops keying every DC it owns to one stat.

Sanctuary.name: Sanctuary & Oathbound
Sanctuary.verdict: Reads as. Two bodies that each bought the recovery the other could not supply and then aimed it outward: a no-action sanctuary laying temporary hit points on the partner every round off a charge the short rest returns, and an aura adding Charisma to every saving throw both halves roll. Under that sits the only revive in the band, a Channel that clears Charm and Fright as it goes, and a whisper package that answers whichever ability an act's gate happens to ask for.
Sanctuary.cost: Costs. Both halves paid for their defence out of their offence — the Rogue gave up its opening skill package, the patron the top of its arcanum — and against this run's inflated health that is a pair which strips enemy turns slowly. The aura is also measured from where the Paladin stands, and a Phantom's whole business is standing somewhere else.

vars.note: A burst engine in place of the aura: it answers the tempo this pairing is short of and takes every save bonus with it when it goes.
Guidance and standing Expertise instead of whispers rationed by the rest, on a body with no armour of its own to keep.

vars.text: Why the deep oath dip: the aura is the entire reason for it and it does not exist until the far end of that stretch, so the shallow version buys heavy armour and saves and stops just short of the thing actually worth paying for.

Conjuration.name: Conjuration & Psalter
Conjuration.verdict: Reads as. Two different primary stats and two different Expertise sources, which is the only way a pair of this size covers checks that are not Charisma — this is the broadest out-of-combat coverage on the board and none of it was bought with combat levels. The exchange in the fight is exact: the Wizard throws healing to the partner as a bonus action off a rest-free conjuring engine, and the Paladin-Bard's aura puts Charisma on every save the Wizard has to make, which is the one thing a body in the back cannot buy for itself.
Conjuration.cost: Costs. Enemy action points come off in a drip. A bonus-action item engine and a table of smites is a lot of turns to remove one boss, and against something with a long health bar the pairing simply takes longer than the fight wants. Neither half wears heavy armour and neither holds a line, so a crowd that closes is standing on top of both bodies at once, with the aura helping the saves and nothing at all helping the hits.

vars.note: Puts a real attack routine in front of the conjurer, at the price of the second skills body the coverage was resting on.
Blinds what closes, which is closer to a front rank than either of these bodies manages.
Keeps the skills and adds the outward blessing, but the tempo drops another rung and it was already the weak half.

Stormcalling.verdict: The lead commits its Action and its concentration to one ten-turn field — Electrifying Aria at 14 repeats a 12m Lightning burst every turn while degrading every caught enemy's Constitution save, until Finale! converts the whole field into a mass Stun — and the partner is the one body in the band whose entire routine costs neither. Fast Hands on top of Lone Wolf's second bonus action is three conjure-and-throw bonus actions a round, all of it slot-free and concentration-free, so the field is never the thing being interrupted and the surfaces stack under it while it ticks. Staying mono is what makes the Aria worth building around: Magical Secrets lands three times for six picks drawn from every list the modlist installs, and the 9th tier arrives. Five damage types between them, and thrown healing potions are the only outward rescue either sheet has.
Stormcalling.cost: Single-target is a hole and the flagged body is flagged on exactly the fights that hole describes — bombs and vials are built for numbers, so against one high-value target the pair fights a body down with nothing to fall back on but a caster whose best work is 12m wide. Single-target reads 3 in Act I and only 5 by Act III. Neither half wears armour or owns any self-mitigation, and resilience never clears 0.55; with no taunt in the game, whatever closes is standing on top of two soft casters. Nothing here lasts either — duration sits at 0.6 in every act.

vars.note: A melee body that maximises the same damage types, which holds the ground two casters cannot and keeps the burst intact.
The front rank this pairing lacks, on a clock that never asks for a long rest — and the skill coverage halves.
An outward blessing and a second Expertise set, on a body no more armoured than the caster it is protecting.

Dirge.name: Dirge & Dawnblind
Dirge.verdict: Reads as. Tragedy rolls any save the pair forces as a Charisma save and the Stare hangs permanent disadvantage on exactly those, for no concentration and no resource, so what the mechanism wants from a partner is saves — as many as it can be handed. Dawnblind deals in them wholesale: an area burst that spares allies and asks every creature it touches for one, spread again from each body that fails, and the failures then take radiant damage for every action they attempt afterwards.
Dirge.cost: Costs. The conversion pays out per save, and this partner delivers its saves in bursts on a short-rest clock rather than round after round, so the mechanism idles between them — the bodies that flood the board every turn are spoken for elsewhere. Neither half wears armour worth the name, nothing here heals outward or raises the other, and against a creature that cannot be blinded the arrangement is two weapon routines.

vars.note: A save that gets worse every turn it persists, rolled at the enemy's worst stat with two penalties on it — the version where the mechanism never idles.
Hazards and saves every round with no slot behind them, and thrown potions, which is the only outward heal any of these leads can reach.

vars.text: None of it is concentration: the Stare is a bonus action and the conversion is passive, so the pair's whole concentration budget stays free for whatever else it wants standing.

Pageant.name: Pageant & Coda
Pageant.verdict: Reads as. Two Bards passing dice in opposite directions: the lead's bond drops a save die on both bodies and its Command repeats off a bonus action for no concentration, while the partner spends its Inspiration and keeps it, so a die goes outward every round from each side. The Peace dip supplies the armour and shields Glamour never gives itself, and the aggro-shed at the top of the College exists for exactly this run, where losing one body ends the fight.
Pageant.cost: Costs. Nothing in the lead's College improves its own damage and the partner's ceiling is a weapon routine and a Charisma cantrip, so this pair talks a fight down rather than ending it, against health totals built to punish that. Both halves are the same class off the same stat besides: every Charisma item is contested, the inspiration economies overlap, and the lead buys its split with a feat the rest of the roster keeps.

vars.note: The kill speed this pairing has none of, at the price of the armour and the melee half the other Bard was holding.
A full Cleric table and the proficiency both mid-run gates are paid in, instead of a second copy of coverage the lead already owns.

vars.text: What the aggro-shed is for: it only pays when there is something worth protecting beside it, and here that is a light-armoured Bard standing in melee with no prevention of its own.

Psalter.verdict: Two outward layers pointed at each other, neither of which spends the pair's concentration. Aura of Protection writes Charisma onto every saving throw both bodies make at Listo's 9m radius, and the body it rescues is the softest thing on the board — a Wizard whose entire turn is bonus actions. Coming back the other way, Fast Hands stacked on Lone Wolf's second bonus action is three conjure-and-throw bonus actions a round, and thrown healing potions reach the partner, so the pair carries an outward heal that costs no slot at all. It is also the strongest skills reading here: Lore Expertise lands in the prologue band and covers town Persuasion at the act's own DC, while Rogue proficiencies and an Intelligence body take Investigation and the trap and cache checks, with Use Best Sleight of Hand handing the host the party-best disarm total. Act I tops the axis and it never drops below 4.
Psalter.cost: The conjurer is flagged on priority fights, and that is the real bill: against a single large target the thrown alchemy is the weakest thing either body does, so every boss is fought with the Bard smiting alone. Single-target damage reads 5 in Act I and 6 after, and tempo peaks at 0.65 and falls back to 0.57 in Act III. Duration is the hole and it does not move — 2 in every act. Neither half wears heavy armour: the oath levels arrive too late for it and the Wizard was never getting it, so the aura the partner has to stand inside is worn on medium at best.

vars.note: A Wisdom body that still clears the Charisma gates, so the pair keeps its coverage and stops paying for a second casting stat.
A full arcane list and resistance-piercing in place of the bonus-action alchemy, which closes the priority-fight flag and ends the rest-free engine.
Arcane Shot riders and a second Lore dip, so the ranged half stops being the softest thing standing in the aura.

Silvercrit.tag: champion moon paladin + snowlight blind ranger
Silvercrit.verdict: A blind engine standing in front of a crit engine, and the two only work because the burst is radiant. Radiance of the Dawn is a short-rest area radiant burst that spares allies, so the armoured half stands inside it while everything else rolls Glaring Frost's Constitution save, and Snowborn Anthelion at Ranger 15 pushes that save three metres past each creature it lands on. Attacking a blinded enemy is advantage, and advantage against Improved Critical's 19–20 takes a swing's crit rate from one in ten to nearly one in five — each crit doubling Divine Smite dice on top of Fount of Moonlight's standing +2d6. Aura of Moonlight and Divine Guardian then point outward at a Ranger that is otherwise the only thing here worth attacking.
Silvercrit.cost: Skills is the hole and it drains across the run: rung 4 in Act I, 3 in Act II, 2 by Act III, with utility down to 0.38 in the back half. Neither half buys Expertise and neither owns Reliable Talent, so as the trap and secret-door band climbs the pair rolls the same flat proficiency it started with. Both halves also deal radiant — the layer that resists it takes the damage and the blind engine off in one roll. Endurance and duration sit at 3 on both bodies because Twilight Sanctuary was sold for Action Surge and the crit range: everything left is priced on the short rest, in a run that charges supplies for it, and the anchor cannot follow a ranged conclave out of the aura that is the whole reason it stands where it stands.

vars.note: A standing temp-HP aura and a ranged damage floor, bought by giving up the second weapon routine.
Lore Expertise and always-prepared Guidance stop the skills fall, on a partner with no armour to lose.
Storm damage on a thrown-weapon Bard, which breaks the shared radiant type at the cost of the control that came with it.

Lectern.verdict: Painful Stare fires once per turn on any damage dealt to the Stare target, and the Monk is the body that guarantees the trigger — a flurry of unarmed strikes at the d12 Martial Arts die means the rider lands every round whether or not its owner spends anything on it. That is a free damage channel the Eyebiter cannot open alone. The skill halves are disjoint in the way this run's check load rewards: Guidance always prepared plus Lore Expertise and three bonus proficiencies on the Wisdom body, Charisma on the other, so traps and doors and town dialogue are covered by a face and a scout rather than two faces. The familiar holds a third initiative slot in a two-body party, and by Mesmerist 10 the Resistance boon covers all damage proportionally on top of Lone Wolf's halving.
Lectern.cost: Act I is the bill. The Lore dip lands at characters 6-8 and the Warlock levels at 9-11, so until then the pair is one strong single-target routine and very little else — no area answer, nothing durable, and almost nothing that takes enemy actions off the board. Tempo reads 0.388 in that act against 0.766 in Act III. Crowds stay a problem for the whole run rather than just the first act: the Monk has nothing wide worth a turn, so every fight against numbers is fought a body down. Skills open at 4 and settle at 3 for both back acts.

vars.note: Puts a standing outward temp-HP layer on a body that wears no armour at all, and gives up the free per-turn damage rider to get it.
An armoured Wisdom body with a real attack routine, which is the shortest route out of the first act's tempo hole.
Buys the missing wide answer outright, and concentrates the pair's whole burst into one element.

Stormthrow.name: Stormthrow & Moonward
Stormthrow.tag: thrown swords bard + mono moon paladin
Stormthrow.verdict: Reads as. One of the few pairings in the ledger with nothing missing — every row clears its bar, skills sit at the top rung across the run, and five damage types spread across two bodies with none doubled. Moonward stacks prevention in layers, a flat subtraction from every hit either body takes and a halving on the partner off a short-rest charge, while the extra Reaction on top of Lone Wolf's own means the Bard's storm rider fires more often than the round should allow.
Stormthrow.cost: Costs. Every outward thing in the pairing is on the Paladin, so the one arrangement this pair cannot survive is the anchor going down — the Bard has nothing to reach across with. The geometry fights itself as well: the aura is measured from where the static body stands, and a thrown-weapon build's whole answer to standing in the middle of a fight is to not be there.

vars.note: The same oath spent on the swing instead of the capstone, so the pair kills faster and the standing prevention thins.
Swaps prevention for a blind engine that stops the hits before they are rolled, and the armour goes with it.

Oathbound.name: Oathbound & Immolate
Oathbound.verdict: Reads as. Two heavy-armoured bodies that both took their martial half first, so neither reads as the soft one the enemy AI picks — and the aura stacks Charisma onto every saving throw both of them make while the Cleric holds no concentration at all to lose. Between them the pairing has an extra Action, a bonus-action strike, smites off short-rest pact slots and a maximised elemental burst, all refilling on the break rather than the supply-priced rest.
Oathbound.cost: Costs. Out of combat this is the blankest pairing in the band — skills clear the opening act and then read at nothing at all for the rest of the run, so every gate after the prologue is met with a raw roll. Both bodies also swing slashing, which is the type the endgame stacks resistance against most casually, and the aura's whole value is measured from where the Warlock stands.

vars.note: A per-turn control rider that spends no action and no concentration, in place of the second armoured routine.
A standing sanctuary underneath the aura, and a third body swinging the same damage type as the first two.
Buys tempo and a second short-rest pool, and gives back every point of armour on that side.

Moonthief.name: Moonthief & Oathbound
Moonthief.verdict: Reads as. Cunning Strike lands a Prone, Poison or Disarm rider every single turn for no action and no concentration, which is the rubric's own top clause for single-target control, and the Wild Shape overhaul keeps every bit of it working inside the beast form. Opposite it stands the heavy-armoured Warlock whose aura adds Charisma to both bodies' saves and whose short-rest pact slots convert straight into smite damage — control that costs nothing beside burst that costs a resource the break returns.
Moonthief.cost: Costs. Nothing here answers a crowd: both halves are single-target machines, one riding a per-turn debuff and the other pointing smites at whatever it is already hitting, so a room is worked through one creature at a time. Skills read at nothing past the opening act as well, and both bodies deal slashing, so the one type the pair leans on hardest is also the one a single resistance layer takes off both at once.

vars.text: Why five levels of Rogue: the short-rest dice pool the other reading buys does the same job worse — Cunning Strike lands its rider unconditionally, where a manoeuvre spends a die to try, and Swashbuckler removes the advantage requirement a two-person party cannot reliably meet.

The aura and the beast form: everything the Warlock gives is measured from where it stands, and a shapeshifter's whole tempo argument is closing distance — the pairing is worth most on the turns both bodies are willing to be in the same place.

Stormlore.name: Stormlore & Moonward
Stormlore.verdict: Reads as. Nothing missing on any row, built from two bodies that each covered the other's blind spot deliberately: a Druid that spent a two-level domain dip on Expertise in two Intelligence proficiencies and at-will Guidance, opposite an oath that is prevention in every form the game sells. Storm Shift still carries its temporary hit points and the immunity-to-resistance clause is untouched, which is the one thing in the pairing that ignores the endgame's layered resistances entirely.
Stormlore.cost: Costs. Tempo is the thinnest in the band — the Paladin is not a damage body and never becomes one, and the Druid gave up the maximised lightning to buy its skills — so this pairing wins by outlasting inflated health rather than removing it, in a run that charges supplies for the rest outlasting depends on. The prevention is also all on one side and measured from where that side stands, and the Druid casts from range.

vars.note: A skirmisher with its own Guidance and Expertise, so the pair stops relying on one body for every check and every save.

vars.text: Knowledge over Tempest: the domain that maximised the lightning also left the Druid at the roster's floor out of combat for the whole run. This trades the spike for the half of the game the Druid list never covered.

Rime.name: Rime & Fontspark
Rime.verdict: Reads as. Glaring Frost forces a Constitution save for Blind on every instance of cold or radiant damage, and the Paladin block exists purely to supply that damage on demand — Divine Smite is radiant, so every smite is a blind attempt, and the effect spreads to everything within a few metres of whatever fails. Fontspark's Twinned wards then cover both bodies from a single cast, and Fey Presence is area control that spends neither slot nor concentration, which is what a blind engine wants standing beside it.
Rime.cost: Costs. Three holes, which is the most in this band: durability, because between draconic scales and a Ranger's leathers there is no armour worth the name; the wide answer, because everything here works one save at a time; and skills, which read at nothing past the opening act. The blind engine is also the whole pairing — meet something that cannot be blinded and this is two ordinary weapon routines and a cantrip.

vars.note: Heavy armour and an aura opposite the blind engine, and the pair's action-free control leaves with the Warlock.
Medium armour, a shield and a die to hand over, which is closer to a front rank than this pairing owns.

Nightwatch.name: Nightwatch & Oathbound
Nightwatch.tag: weapon twilight cleric + old one paladin-lock
Nightwatch.verdict: Reads as. The most heavily armoured pairing in the ledger, and both halves earned it the same way — martial levels taken first, so neither reads as the target the enemy AI opens on. Twilight Sanctuary runs as a no-concentration aura putting temporary hit points on both bodies every round off a short-rest charge, and the Warlock's aura stacks Charisma onto every save underneath it, with Revivify sitting behind both as the only real floor either body has.
Nightwatch.cost: Costs. Two of the three damage types in this pairing are on both bodies at once — the same slashing weapons and the same radiant rider — which means a single resistance layer takes most of the pair's output off simultaneously, and Absolute Wrath is on. Out of combat it reads at nothing past the opening act, nothing here answers a crowd, and both bodies want to be standing in the same place for their respective auras to matter.

vars.note: The pairing's skills problem answered directly, at the cost of the second suit of heavy armour.
Prevention in place of the aura, which does not stack with it — and the pair's damage thins further.
A blessing and a revive on a Wisdom body, and the front rank halves.

Seelie.verdict: Two control engines pointed at two different saves, and the second one is what a blind engine standing alone never has. Glaring Frost forces a Constitution save for Blind on every instance of cold or radiant damage, the Paladin block at characters 4-6 is taken purely to supply that damage on demand — Divine Smite is radiant, so every smite is a blind attempt — and Snowborn Anthelion spreads the save to everything within 3 m of whatever fails, with Snow Blindness taxing every action the survivors take. Attacks against a blinded creature have advantage, and this is the body built to cash that in: Action Surge on an Eldritch Blast chassis is eight beams in one turn, every one of them rolling twice. The other engine costs nothing to run — Fey Presence is area charm-or-fear off a short-rest charge that spends neither a slot nor concentration, and Dominate Person at patron 9 lands on a short-rest pact slot rather than a long-rest one — so something that cannot be blinded still owes a Wisdom save. Out of combat the two bodies cover different halves of the board, Charisma for town dialogue and a Ranger's Wisdom for traps and caches, which opens skills at 4 in Act I, about as high as a two-body party gets.
Seelie.cost: The wide answer is the hole and the flagged body makes it worse: the area row never climbs, and the Ranger has nothing worth doing against a crowd, so every crowd fight is fought a body down — one Warlock working one target at a time while the other half swings. Rescue is the second hole, at 2, 3, 2: nothing on the Warlock is aimed at the partner at all, and the pairing's only outward answer is the Revivify a Ranger does not reach until class 9, with no prevention, no condition removal and no outward heal on either side. Fighter 3 buys the armour and the extra beams by trading away the Wisdom and Charisma save proficiencies for Strength and Constitution, which is the wrong pair to own against an endgame that throws Wisdom saves. Skills fall from 4 to 2 for Acts II and III as the dialogue and detection bands climb past both bodies, and durability sits at 3 in every act — light armour and no shield on one, leathers on the other, and no third body to stand in front of either.

vars.note: A maximised Fireball twice per short rest, which is the wide answer this pairing never buys — and the blind engine leaves with the Ranger.
Heavy armour and an every-round temp-HP aura aimed outward, in place of the second control engine and the Ranger's half of the skill board.
Medium armour, a shield and a die to hand over, plus the Expertise that keeps the skills row from falling off after Act I.

cards.title: Coverage is derived, not chosen
cards.body: The roster is not a shortlist. Every ### heading in the seventeen class files was enumerated mechanically — 157 — and each had to come back with a verdict. Two were headings over a table rather than a subclass. One was rejected for having no published progression. Three more proved unbuildable. The rest produced 170 bodies. A subclass missing from this ledger is missing because someone wrote down why.

cards.title: Two passes, and the second one chooses the split
cards.body: The first pass scores each subclass as a mono-twenty body — the zero-dip reference point, not a recommendation. The second pass takes that profile, the axis rubric and every class's dip table, and decides what twenty levels this subclass should actually be. Splitting it that way matters: the previous ledger let a stage with no rubric in front of it pick the most consequential number on the page, and it came back three-quarters mono-class.

cards.title: Dipping is nearly free here, and the roster shows it
cards.body: Feats key off character level in this list, so a three-level dip costs none. Lone Wolf already grants two save proficiencies, so the classic Fighter 1 for Constitution buys nothing. What a dip costs is only the top of the abandoned class table — and outside a handful of real capstones that is very little. Fifteen of 170 bodies are mono-class, and each names the specific late feature that beat the best three levels available elsewhere.

cards.title: Ten axes, three acts, four blocks
cards.body: Each body carries ten values per act against a written rubric. Each axis has a 0–5 ladder for what kind of capability a rung is, and an act table for what it must be in each act to hold that rung. Act I is characters 3–8, II is 9–15, III is 16–20. The four blocks — Tempo, Resilience, Duration, Utility — are the reporting surface; there is no single total, on purpose.

cards.title: Rungs re-baseline, so most axes do not move
cards.body: A 5 in Act I means as good as a body can be at character 8, not as good as a body ever gets. So a body with Extra Attack and a rider is a 3 in every act — it has not got worse, the world moved with it. Movement is close to symmetric here: 271 axis values rise across the run and 243 fall, with 1,016 flat. The previous ledger managed 883 rises to 34 falls, which is what an absolute ladder looks like rather than a run.

cards.title: Two axes are evidence, for opposite reasons
cards.body: Saves and Skills are both derived rather than authored, and the reasons are mirror images. Saves are personal: each body rolls its own, so a Wisdom proficiency on one character does nothing for the other and the pair is its weakest link. Skills are shared: Use Highest Modifier in dialogue reads every party member's total and boosts whoever is rolling to the party maximum, so a gate falls if either body clears it. Neither has a combining operator on the rung, because the combination happens on the evidence — a proficiency set, a modifier — before a rung exists. That also retires an error: the old operator normalised Skills against seven, so a pair where one body cleared every gate scored 0.71 while the host was in fact rolling at the party maximum and clearing all of them.

cards.title: Skills means the checks you cannot prepare for
cards.body: The axis used to score the run's named gates. That was the wrong target twice over. Withers charges 100 gold and sits in the Dank Crypt from Act I, and bg3.wiki documents respeccing into Rogue 11 / Knowledge Cleric 1 for Religion Expertise, passing the Mirror of Loss at DC 25, then respeccing back retaining the stat enhancement — so the Mirror measured a wallet and is no longer scored. Worse, every named gate has a no-check route to the same reward: taking Ethel's deal yields the hair and costs only Mayrina, and Araj can be killed and looted. Passing buys the secondary prize, never the ability point. What survives both objections is the untelegraphed half, scored every act: traps and hidden caches (Perception 15–25), secret doors and switches (Investigation 15–20), and routine town dialogue (Persuasion, at the act's own band — 10–15, 15–18, 18–22). These fire without warning in whatever build is worn, so they measure the chassis. Hag's Hair and the Araj pickpocket are still scored beside them. Each check takes the pair's better body, and the rung is the mean clear probability across the act, capped when any single check is near-hopeless — a check nobody can roll is a different failure from one everyone rolls badly. Inspiration counts on the named gates only: traps roll automatically with no prompt, and four charges do not stretch across a run of town dialogue.

cards.title: Every pair, then the frontier
cards.body: There is no carry/support partition. All 170 chassis are paired with all others — 14,365 pairings — and the entries are the Pareto frontier over the four blocks: 127 pairings that nothing beats on all four at once. 44 chassis appear somewhere on it. Everything else is dominated rather than deleted, and the field table keeps the highest-scoring of them as the record.

cards.title: Nothing quoted is hand-written
cards.body: Every figure here — scores, block percentages, utilisation, variation lines — is computed at render time from about 5,000 authored integers. The largest source of error in the first ledger was hand-copied numbers going stale after a re-score. Here they cannot, because they do not exist until the page is built.

cards.title: What the frontier actually rewards
cards.body: Selection is a Pareto frontier over four blocks, and Pareto is invariant to how you weight a dimension — only to how many dimensions there are and what is in them. Tempo holds four axes, Resilience three, and Duration and Utility hold one each. So skl and end each carry a quarter of the dominance test while st carries a sixteenth. In practice a body must be best at something, and Skills is the cheapest place to be best: across this roster frontier membership correlates with mean Skills at +0.75, against +0.17 for Endurance and −0.30 for Durability. A body under 1 on Skills reaches the frontier 12% of the time; a body at 3 or above, 60%. That is not a fault in the blocks — two characters carry every proficiency the run will ever have, which is why the model weights Skills 2.5 — but it is invisible from four block names, so it is stated here.

cards.title: Bodies are checked against their own subclass
cards.body: The model already refuses a value it does not recognise — an unknown booster id or reach raises rather than being skipped. Nothing used to check a value that was simply omitted: an effect that exists, has a registry id, is reachable at this body's level, and is not recorded. That is the same invisible failure, because a missing booster contributes nothing and a score that is too low reads exactly like an honest one. Every built body is now cross-checked against the tier-1 profile of its own subclass, which knows what that subclass contributes alone. It is a subset test, never an equality test: sibling variants are meant to differ, and anything extra came from the dip. Two omissions were found and corrected, and eleven bodies were flagged for a judgement their record had not stated.

cards.title: Weaknesses are priced, not just printed
cards.body: A pairing's holes and idle bodies used to be collected, drawn as chips, and left out of the score — the page could say idles in crowd fights directly above a result the chip had not touched. Both now cost. A flagged body multiplies that fight type's term in that act by 0.85, because the pair fights it a body down; a hole multiplies the block it belongs to by 0.95, once per axis per act, because with two characters there is no third to cover a gap. Both are deliberately small, since the raw effect is already partly counted — the idle body's zero is in the damage sum and the holed axis is in its block's average. These price the structural remainder. The effect is real but not violent: fourteen of the top twenty rows are unchanged, while the top twenty-five's mean flag count falls by a third and the pairings that rise are the ones with no idle body at all.

cards.title: Two bodies are not two of the same body
cards.body: Three pair-level facts the model used to miss. Damage type: Absolute Wrath layers resistance on ordinary enemies, and two bodies dealing the same type have no answer when it lands — a duo holding one type between them is charged, two is charged less, three or more is free. Single-source rescue: an outward answer that lives entirely on one body is not the same as two bodies carrying half each, because when the body that heals is the body that went down, nothing picks it up. Contention: two bodies of the same class want the same unique items and the same ability spread, which is charged as a deliberately coarse proxy for something the model cannot see properly. Together they moved same-class pairings from a quarter of the top twenty-five to none of it.

caveats.h2: What this ledger does not know

excluded.summary: Enumerated and rejected, with the reason
items: Inquisitor — Tactics, Vengeance and Zeal are structurally unbuildable, not merely weak. Subclasses are chosen at level 3 and the shipped install has a dangling subclass GUID there, so a split must stop at Inquisitor 2 — and at 2 there is no subclass at all. The mod needs updating to 2.2.1.
Sorcerer / Wretched Soul — no published feature list, levels or progression. The class file marks the whole subclass unverified and Listo added it for testing.
Cleric's heavy-armour table and Paladin's Oath Framework parse as headings but are not subclasses — a twenty-row proficiency matrix and a modder API respectively.
excluded.lead: Three of 157 headings produced no body and three more were not subclasses. They are listed so a gap reads as a decision rather than an oversight.

settled.summary: Settled by reading the installed paks
items: Eldritch Blast is 1d8 per beam in this list, not 1d10. Any damage arithmetic imported from outside Listo is overstated.
Eldritch Cone and Line stop scaling at character 10 — LevelMapValue(EldritchZoneDamage) ends at 3d10 — and the cone's success roll never checks Agonizing Blast.
Combat Extender runs at +126% regular and +170% boss HP, which is what makes a flat, non-upcasting feature fall across the acts rather than merely stand still.
Absolute Wrath is on, so ordinary enemies carry layered resistances. A body locked to one commonly-resisted damage type caps at 4 on single-target from Act II.
Save DCs decay against the curve: bosses gain +1 spell save DC per 7 levels, ordinary enemies +1 per 11. Pure save-DC control loses a rung by Act III; imposing disadvantage does not.
Feats land at character 3/6/9/12/13/15/18, plus 11 for Fighter and Rogue. Every individual mod page's own feat table is wrong for this list — which is also why a dip here costs no feats.

Only the level-1 class grants saving throws, and for several classes only it grants the good armour. Each split records which class is first, because it changes the save set and therefore the highest-weighted axis in the model.

assumptions.summary: Assumptions that would still move numbers
items: Forty-two of 170 bodies rest partly on sources that are not the installed pak. The worst are named in their own notes: Ordnance (School of Bombardment) and Vantage (War Magic) have image-only feature tables and are scored as the bare Wizard chassis with nothing credited to the school; Dreamwarden (Circle of Dreams) and Dawnwright (Oath of Illumination) likewise carry nothing from their own subclass. Read those four rows as floors, not scores.

The first pass chose one dip per class, not per subclass. Batching scoring agents by class amortised the reading but produced herding: 12 of 16 Wizards took the same Cleric 1, 8 of 12 Druids the same Cleric 3, and every Druid scored identically on Skills — zero variance across twelve bodies is a class default, not twelve readings. A second pass built an alternative dip for every chassis on the frontier and for every class showing that pattern, which is where this ledger's variants come from. The first-pass bodies were not rebuilt, so a subclass whose best expression needs an unherded dip may still be represented by the herded one.

The variant pass was pointed at the axis the selector rewards, and that is a circularity worth naming. Analysis of the previous ledger found frontier membership correlating with Skills at +0.75, and the variant brief then told agents that Skills was the axis nobody had built for. They duly built for it — mean Skills across the 95 variants is 2.33 against 1.50 for the first-pass bodies — and 31 of the 40 bodies in the top twenty entries are variants. The builds are legitimate and the gap they filled was real: twelve Druids had scored identically on Skills and the best Barbarian of fourteen had scored 0.7. But a reader should know that attention was directed at that axis rather than arrived at independently, and that a selector rewarding Skills and a pass optimising Skills will agree with each other by construction.

Blanket save effects still outrun the registry. It grew from three ids to 24 during this build, but the grants pass turned up more that have no id and therefore contribute nothing — Inquisition's Spell Shield, Zealous Presence, Star Druid's Cosmic Omen among them. The error is one-directional: those bodies read too low, never too high.

Anointed in Splendour is not modelled. It is +2 to every saving throw, purchasable, per character. Being available to every body it does not move any ranking, but it means the Saves axis sits one flat step low in absolute terms across the whole ledger.

Frontier membership inherits provisional weights. Dominance over four blocks is ordinal and fairly robust, but the Resilience block's internal weighting — saves 3.0 down to rescue 1.5 — decides which pairings survive. Change those and the 127 changes.

Splits are one honest reading, not a search. Each was chosen by an agent holding that subclass's mono-twenty profile, the rubric and every class's dip table. An attempt to search the space mechanically instead — composing splits from a catalogue of what each class's levels buy — was built and then rejected: the catalogue's per-class scales varied fourfold between authors, which put whichever class had been scored most generously into every 'optimal' build. The catalogue survives as reference prose; its arithmetic does not.

Two bodies carry a pairing constraint no axis can express. Path of the Revenant cannot be healed by any means while raging, which makes it inert opposite a healer rather than merely suboptimal; Order of the Lycan's Bloodlust sends it at its own partner below half health, and advantage on that save only arrives at character 18.

Eleven bodies are flagged on concentration and not resolved. Each is an expression of a subclass whose tier-1 profile records that its plan rides a concentration spell, while the body itself says it does not. That can be a legitimate build — a weapon-primary Cleric need never hold one — but none of the eleven said so, and the difference decides whether a pair has one free concentration slot or none. Three further bodies were corrected outright rather than flagged: they took Way of the Friar, whose Bond is explicitly Concentration in the class file, and three sibling Friar bodies had flagged it while these three had not. Two of those three may now be a rung high on control, since the rung-4 clause on both control axes is specifically control that costs no concentration.

Holes and idle bodies are the norm, not the exception, and the penalty is calibrated for that. Every one of the 34,980 pairings carries at least one hole and 94% carry at least one flag; the median pairing has three holes and two flags. So a pairing with one hole is a good pairing, not a flawed one, and the chips should be read against that base rate rather than against zero. The penalty is exponential in the count for exactly this reason — it separates the two-hole pairing from the six-hole one rather than punishing the existence of a hole.

Race and background are not modelled, so every Skills rung is a floor. The roster records a split and nothing about the character carrying it, and a background alone grants two proficiencies — Acolyte, for instance, grants Religion, the skill behind the run's hardest gate. Every modifier here is therefore conservative by up to two proficiencies, uniformly. Relative ordering survives that, because proficiency on a dumped ability is still nowhere near DC 25, but a rung should be read as what the chassis guarantees rather than as a ceiling.

Skills rung 5 is unreachable, and that is a finding rather than a gap. The best pair in the field averages 0.79 against a 0.75 threshold, but Perception against the 15–25 trap band peaks at 0.60 for anyone on this roster, and the worst-check cap holds the rung down. No two-character party covers this run's detection load, so the axis runs 0–4 in practice and a 4 should be read as excellent rather than adequate. Separately, proficiency bonus is pinned at +3/+4/+5 by act across all nine recorded skills; strict rules give +6 for characters 17–20. Rescoring on that convention moves 5 of the top 20 and changes the Act III rung on 87 of 265 chassis, though no pairing moves more than 0.9 points. The pin is uniform and internally consistent; correcting it means re-deriving every skill.
